decision: Every Rust tool in the commons declares its invocation surface - arguments and environment - with argenv, the commons' own crate: ocoeco, tad, the engine, devlab and tone move from clap, one at a time, proven equal (the same commands and environment behaviour).
why: The author asked whether all our tools use argenv; only lab-agent and snapall did. clap was chosen by default without looking inside the commons first; argenv gives one declared, typed, machine-readable contract for argv and env, readable by agents and by ocoeco.
rejected: Keeping clap (a second way to declare a surface, and environment read by hand).

decision: Every change carries a record made by ocoeco (a changes table in the shared language), the commit message is rendered from it, and ocoeco release consumes the records to set the version, write release notes tied to milestones and backlog, and tag - taking over from release-please and release-plz. The guarantee is at the boundaries that cannot be skipped: land refuses a change with no record, and a CI check on every pull request does the same; a local hook only points the way. Local commits stay free; the record is per change. Refined the same day by 2026-11-11-glimpses: the record is the glimpse, made while the work is fresh; a change is the glimpses it carries.
why: The author: data about work goes stale because nothing guarantees it is produced; release tooling writes prose nobody consumes, while ocoeco already knows tasks, goals, decisions and effort. 48% of recent landings produced any data.
rejected: Records only in commit messages (lost to squash merges, readable only through git); refusing every local commit with hooks (they fight rebase and amend, are bypassed with --no-verify, and the bypass becomes routine); adopting changesets or Knope as they are (a bump and a summary, tied to nothing else); keeping release-please (prose that drives nothing).

decision: ocoeco check reads a project's essence as advice and never fails on a gap.
why: A gap is the truth about a project, not an error in its data.
rejected: Failing the check until every step is served.

decision: Code is changed by structure: whole items replaced with ast-grep, matched by their signature; logic kept outside macros where tools and readers see it; new views and tools added as new files; every edit verified before anything lands.
why: Patching source by matching text was the heaviest manual work (19 times) and the cause of most failed runs, one of which landed a commit that changed nothing.
rejected: Text patches with better anchors; Comby (language-agnostic, less exact for Rust); writing our own rewriter.

decision: Hand-work saturation is measured in effort - minutes weighted by load on Borg's CR10 scale - as well as count; there is no deliberate status: looking, listening and deciding are counted and automatable like the rest.
why: The author's 30 kg box: ten seconds, yet draining. And tests must judge sound and pictures themselves, with no person judging mid-run (jidoka).
rejected: Count alone; NASA-TLX's six ratings on every bump (too heavy); exempting judgment from automation.

decision: The record of work is the glimpse, made through ocoeco at any moment while the work is fresh; ocoeco supplies most of it (what ocoeco note wrote since the last glimpse, the backlog items and milestones they serve, the effort), and the person or agent types a line. ocoeco commit renders a commit from the glimpses not yet committed, with a trailer per glimpse; ocoeco release consumes the glimpses of what has landed. Git depends on ocoeco, never the reverse: a glimpse needs no git.
why: The author: capture data where it is fresh, while the work is remembered, not sorted out afterwards; and git operations depend on ocoeco, not ocoeco on git. This refines 2026-11-11-changes-are-records, whose record was tied to a change.
rejected: One record per change, written at commit time (later than the work, and tied to git); records only in commit messages; hooks refusing every local commit.

decision: Hand-work becomes part of ocoeco's language: a handwork table of atomic actions with counts, recorded by ocoeco hand (match, bump, or ask), shown by the observatory as hand-work worth a tool.
why: Proposed by the author. A board task is many steps and never repeats; atomic actions do. The wording is kept from drifting by the tool, as the vocabulary keeps words from drifting.
rejected: Logging whole tasks (they never repeat); free-text notes in the session log (they cannot be counted); bumping on any resemblance without asking (silent merging of different actions).

decision: ocoeco check names every table a repository keeps beside its exported ones but does not export.
why: A device lab's whole backlog and a tool's decisions and log went unseen by the observatory for days; ocoeco note found it by refusing.
rejected: Exporting every file automatically - some are kept for a project's own use.

decision: The shared language is language.toml, a tad declaration; ocoeco note checks each row it writes with tad's check_row; the shapes kept as Rust constants are gone.
why: One way to declare and check tables across the commons: tad's, readable by people and by any tool. A test proved the file said exactly what the constants said before they were removed; ocoeco's own tests pass unchanged.
rejected: Rewriting every project's tables in tad's canonical form now (churn in 22 projects, no reader gains); keeping the shapes in Rust (a second declaration language).

decision: Hand-work is called manual work everywhere - the table manual_work, the command ocoeco manual, land --manual; every record and bump appends a timed event to manual_events.
why: The author: manual work is the plain word, and with the time kept it can be set beside commits and releases. A command named manual could be read as documentation; the vocabulary defines it, and ocoeco has no documentation command to collide with.
rejected: hand-work (less plain); ocoeco did (the person does, not the tool); inventing times for the history recorded before.

decision: Rows are recorded with ocoeco note, not hand-written per job.
why: Every job wrote its own script to patch JSON: the same handwork again and again, each a chance to break a table. On its first use the tool found that ocoeco itself exported no decisions.
rejected: A per-job script; a general JSON editor that knows nothing of the format.

decision: ocoeco manual without an action opens a list in the terminal (ratatui): type to narrow, arrows, Enter, the usual minutes and load offered.
why: Asked by the author: typing an action again is a chore and splits the ledger into near-duplicates.
rejected: A web form (not TTY-first); fuzzy matching on typed text alone (it guesses).

decision: Research joins the language as its own table (question, found, sources, date); decisions cite it and name the steps they are about; the observatory badges each step with its decisions.
why: Asked by the author: research should back decisions visibly, beside the milestones and progress they concern, and looking around should be a practice for agents and humans alike.
rejected: Sources alone (a list of works says nothing of the question asked); a separate research page with no link to steps.

decision: Any row may be researched rather than live: it cites a research entry and is drawn outlined, with its age and a link; research gains versions (topic, date, supersedes), a refresh horizon, and a place in the attention view when it goes stale.
why: Asked by the author, to fill the picture honestly with what others achieved.
rejected: Copying outside claims in as if measured; overwriting research on refresh; marking live data (live is the default).

decision: Vocabulary becomes part of ocoeco's language: a vocabulary table (term, means, not, see), the shared words defined by ocoeco itself, a project's own words beside them, translated like everything else, and shown in views.
why: Asked for by the author, so the work can be spoken about clearly; concepts and vocabulary answer different questions.
rejected: Folding definitions into the concepts table; a glossary written by the observatory about projects.

decision: Where the whole is weakest right now is where attention goes.
why: What should be looked at next, read from every project - not what is loudest.
rejected: triage (medical jargon); focus; priorities (a ranking someone sets)

decision: An idea a project rests on, with why it matters, is a concept.
why: Distinct from idea (why the project exists) and from vocabulary (what a word means).
rejected: principle (a rule to follow, a narrower thing); belief

decision: A shared process that projects call, not copy, is a conveyor.
why: A conveyor carries any load the same way; you put work on it, you do not build your own.
rejected: pipeline (CI jargon, and one run); template (copied, the opposite)

decision: A lens chosen to stand in the observatory's navigation is curated.
why: Says chosen with care, and nothing more; any lens is still found without it.
rejected: featured, pinned (web jargon); official (claims an authority it does not have)

decision: An owned fork pinned upstream and changed only as patches meant to go home is a cutting.
why: Rhizoid's gardening word: a cutting is a living piece of the parent plant, grown in your soil.
rejected: fork (suggests drifting apart); vendored copy (a frozen copy, nothing goes home)

decision: A choice taken, with why and what was rejected, is a decision.
why: The plain word; the rejected options are what make it worth keeping.
rejected: ADR (an acronym a reader must be taught); choice (says nothing of the alternatives)

decision: Minutes weighted by load are effort.
why: Effort is the plain word for time and strain together - the 30 kg box.
rejected: cost (money); toil score (jargon); workload (NASA-TLX's wider measure)

decision: A project's whole chain on one page is its essence.
why: Essence is what a thing most truly is; the page shows why, what, how and now at once.
rejected: overview, summary (say less, not more); dashboard (numbers, no reasons); at a glance

decision: The daily job that writes down what a project's work produced is its gatherer.
why: One metaphor, kept whole: gatherers in each field, the harvest brought in by the observatory.
rejected: collector (monitoring jargon); logger; recorder (plain, but breaks the metaphor)

decision: The observatory's reading of every marked project is the harvest.
why: It brings in what the gatherers gathered; the pair is easy to keep in mind.
rejected: crawl, scrape (say how, not what); sync; import

decision: The three stretches of a path are horizons.
why: Horizons are near and far at once - working, perfection and ongoing perfection are all in view together.
rejected: phase, stage (imply one ends before the next begins); level (sounds like a score)

decision: Why a project exists, told for anyone, is its idea.
why: The everyday word; a reader knows what an idea is without being taught.
rejected: vision, mission (corporate jargon); pitch (selling); purpose (narrower)

decision: A grand view of a family of projects, declared as a small file, is a lens.
why: You look through a lens; many lenses can look at the same commons, and anyone may make one.
rejected: view (every page is a view - two meanings); dashboard; portal

decision: How draining an action was this time is its load.
why: Short and physical, as in carrying a load; one number from Borg's CR10.
rejected: exertion (formal); fatigue (an aftermath, not the act); difficulty

decision: The file by which a repository joins the commons is a mark.
why: Short and plain: a mark is something you put on a thing to say what it belongs to.
rejected: manifest (a package's description elsewhere - two meanings); badge (a picture); tag (GitHub topics are only half of it)

decision: A step on a path is a milestone, reached only when its evidence exists.
why: The word readers know; the vocabulary adds only the rule that evidence reaches it, not a date.
rejected: step (too small to name a stretch of work); goal (aims, not proves); checkpoint

decision: The mirror that reads and draws the commons is the observatory.
why: One watches from an observatory and changes nothing: the mirror, not the control centre.
rejected: dashboard, portal, hub (suggest control)

decision: The commons' language and machinery keep their own name, ocoeco.
why: A proper name, chosen by the author: the observatory's ecosystem - the blood and heart.
rejected: a descriptive name (it is the name of a thing, not a description)

decision: What a project must reach is its path.
why: A path is walked step by step and says nothing of dates - exactly a list of milestones with their evidence.
rejected: roadmap (promises dates, a second meaning we do not want); plan; route

decision: A repository with a mark is a project.
why: The plain word everyone already uses; one repository, one project, one mark.
rejected: repository (says where, not what); module; component

decision: The look around before acting is research.
why: The everyday word for looking into something before deciding.
rejected: prior art (the sources, not the looking); investigation; due diligence (legal)

decision: Manual work done often or heavily enough to ask for a tool is saturated.
why: The author's own word; it says full - nothing more should be carried by hand.
rejected: overdue (blames); hot spot (jargon)

decision: A work a project stands on is a source.
why: The word readers know from any citation.
rejected: reference (also means a pointer); citation (the act, not the work)

decision: The words a project speaks and exactly what they mean are its vocabulary.
why: A vocabulary is a language spoken - the ubiquitous language of domain-driven design - not a list kept at the back.
rejected: glossary (a list at the back of a book); dictionary; terminology (formal)

decision: What actually happens is work: the backlog, the log, what the gatherers record.
why: Plain, and set against the plan; the Essence page asks of it: what is happening now.
rejected: activity (only commits); progress (a judgment, not a record)

decision: How the steps are delivered and proven are its workings, as in the workings of a clock; a single entry is called by its kind.
why: Workings is everyday English for the parts that make something work. Working as a singular noun is unusual and was the weakest word in the language.
rejected: working (unusual as a noun); means (plain, but it would collide with the vocabulary's own means field - one word, two meanings); mechanism (sounds like code only); instrument

decision: Words are chosen like decisions: a vocabulary entry names the decision that chose it, the decision records the words rejected and cites research; every vocabulary is reviewed this way.
why: Asked by the author: wording is part of perfection. A word is how everyone after us will think about the thing.
rejected: Definitions without reasons; leaving the words as they first came.

decision: There is not one observatory. OCO is the ecosystem - the agreement (ocoeco) and its tools - that lets anyone have one. A constellation has its own fulldome; an observatory is someone's place where the fulldomes they care about come together, and observatories can be brought together, one gathering others. Observer and observatory named one thing: observatory is kept. The author's observatory - where his own constellations come together - is one of many, to be parted from OCO the ecosystem, with which it is mixed today in one organization. Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-places-lenses-acts: observer is kept after all, as the part of ocoeco that observes - an act, not a place.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the point of OCO is that it is not one observatory; anyone will be able to create theirs, and all or some can be brought together to share their views of the sky; OCO as a project had got mixed with his own projects. An observatory that can gather others needs no special home above it - the same thing, nested, as Ostrom found lasting commons to be.
rejected: One observatory for everyone (a centre the commons would then depend on); a special home of observers above observatories (an observatory gathering others is enough); two words, observer and observatory, for one thing; parting the author's observatory from the ecosystem at once (a careful move, later).

decision: OCO is three kinds of things. Places, where data lives (git repositories today): a star produces; a constellation is a family of stars that belong together, gathering their data and keeping what holds between them; an observatory is someone's looking, gathering what they care to see. Ways of seeing: a lens - the data it needs, where it comes from, how it is shown - made once and used by anyone; and the fulldome, the outermost lens, the same for every place over whatever it holds. Acts of ocoeco: record (a star producing its data where things are fresh), observe (the observer: gathering from other places, the same at every scale) and show (running lenses). The observer brings data and the names of lenses; since a lens shows the same data the same way anywhere, taking a ready render is a shortcut, not a principle.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: star, constellation and observatory come from the need for places; without the constellation the relations between projects have nowhere to live; the fulldome is the board taken to its full potential, realized in ocoeco's structure and lenses; a lens, once done, just works for anyone in ocoeco; the observer finds its place in ocoeco as what allows the gathering of gatherings. Sorting the words by kind shows the same shape at every scale (the-same-at-every-scale).
rejected: Star and observatory alone (belonging and looking are different claims: one about the stars, one about the looker); the fulldome as one lens beside the others (it would no longer be the whole); the fulldome as something other than a lens (a second mechanism); observer as a second word for observatory (2026-11-12-many-observatories is refined: it is an act of ocoeco, not a place); a lens that must bring its own instruments (a plugin system); observatories gathering only renders (a view of the whole needs the data).

decision: Reflection is an entity of the shared language (language.toml): id, date, by, over, saw, learned, changes, answers (other reflections) and touches (decisions, practices, backlog, research, glimpses - table:id in this project, project/table:id in another). Reflections are written into the data like everything else, so whoever comes next - a person or a machine - inherits the lessons, not only the state.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: reflect upon all that was done, as an entity related to the others. A session's lessons otherwise live in a conversation that ends; ocoeco is the place that lasts.
rejected: Keeping reflections in the session log (a log says what was done, in order; a reflection says what it meant, across a stretch); a reflection per project only (a look back often spans several, so it touches across projects); a separate field for each voice (each voice is its own reflection, and answers the other).

decision: The relations of the shared language are declared as data (relations.toml): which field refers to which table - twelve, among them two that were missing: a decision refining or replacing another (decisions.refines) and work serving a milestone or decision (backlog.serves). ocoeco check verifies every link within a star, and with --root the links into other stars. A field holds several links separated by commas or spaces; table:id names the table; project/table:id points into another star.
why: The fulldome is one sky only if what is connected is truly connected (research the-fulldome-lens-by-lens, ocoeco-as-a-database): about 860 links were kept by discipline alone. On 2026-11-12 one decision refining another was written as prose eight times over.
rejected: Leaving relations to discipline; rewriting existing data to one separator (glimpses use spaces, reflections commas: both are read); putting the relations into tad's declaration now (tad's own references rule does not read lists or table:id yet - it should, later).

decision: ocoeco's acts are record, observe and show. Observe replaces harvest and discover. Record stays plain. Show stays plain until the first lens is built and run; shine is kept in mind for it.
why: One word, one meaning; a word someone can guess from what it does (research the-words-for-the-acts).
rejected: pulse for record (taken by oco-agent's pulse, and it cannot be guessed); shine for show now (it reads as either of two acts); naming an act before touching it.

decision: The board is a view over every project's backlog (ocoeco board), never a list of its own. The backlog carries the flow - open, next, in-progress, waiting, parked, done, dropped - and four optional fields: driver (who holds it), next (its next step), since (the day it entered its state), waits_on. The board shows in progress by driver, waiting and on what, next, and what needs attention: more than three held by one driver, in progress with no next step or nobody holding it, nothing moved for a week. oco-agent speaks it when it changes. Refined the same day by 2026-11-12-the-room: the flow of work is one lens of the room, not the room.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: the board must come from ocoeco's data, with ocoeco and oco-agent developed hand in hand, after the best research. One truth: the backlog is already kept in every project as the work goes; a second list is a second truth that drifts (lab-agent's board was one).
rejected: A board kept as its own list (lab-agent's board.json: a second truth); a column per project (the flow is the point, not where an item lives); priorities as numbers or points (the order is the next state, pulled; time is measured as age instead of estimated); hill charts now (worth adding once the flow is lived).

decision: The whole is called the fulldome, not the room, and it has no walls: a part of it is a lens, and what is connected - a decision, its research, the work it caused, the result - is seen as connected. The fulldome shows the story (why a star exists, what it must reach, how, what is happening), time (the sky on any date: the data's own history) and intent, and it is touched and acted in, not watched. What a lens and a render are is not a protocol beside ocoeco: it is ocoeco - the shared language and the mark grow to say them, and ocoeco's tools read, check and write them, so a star follows the agreement by using ocoeco, not by remembering it.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: room and wall do not fit the whole; a planetarium's dome shows not only constellations but the story behind them, relations, a history, intent; and ocoeco is the agreement and a convenient way to follow it automatically - not principles on paper, a ritual, or a discipline in someone's head. Fulldome belongs with star, constellation, lens, observer and observatory; a dome is one continuous sky, where walls divide.
rejected: Room and wall (2026-11-12-the-room keeps its substance; its words are replaced); a render agreement as a protocol of its own (rules to read and remember: the thing ocoeco exists to make unnecessary); a fulldome one only watches (a planetarium's audience: the open commons' must invite).

decision: A board is the room, not a list: the open commons' obeya, where anyone sees the whole. ocoeco's entities are its walls, and a wall is a lens. OCO is described by four words: a star (one idea or project keeping its own ocoeco data), a constellation (stars seen together), a lens (queries and how they are shown, over the same data), an observer (gathers renders, renders nothing of others again); OCO is the home of observers. The flow of work built as ocoeco board is one lens of the room, not the room. A view across stars is a lens of their constellation, rendered once there from the stars' data, so observers still only gather renders; and a render carries a small agreement - its lens, its format, where it starts - so an observer can place it. Lenses declared as data replace three things planned apart: the renderer leaving tad, presentation as data, and the observatory engine's hand-written views. Its words are replaced the same day by 2026-11-12-the-fulldome: the whole is the fulldome, and a part of it is a lens, not a wall.
why: The author, 2026-11-12: ocoeco is the next step, for open commons, of the room where everyone sees the whole - as a principle, a system and an implementation - learnt by seeing and touching, not by cramming; too much had been centred on the backlog; and words are added only where they reflect the whole and make it simpler. The research (the-room) shows the walls are already here, and that the author's four words and the room are one design.
rejected: The board as a view over the backlog alone (one wall taken for the room: 2026-11-12-the-board is refined by this); a board entity of its own; observers rendering stars' data themselves (a star owns how it is shown, and no star may need an observer to be seen); a framework's ceremonies and score boards; adding words that name no distinct part of the whole.
